content: Warwick Medical School is located at one of the United Kingdom's leading research universities, the University of Warwick, which consistently ranks in the top 10 of the Times University ratings. The school was established in 2000 as part of a government initiative to address the shortage of doctors in Britain. Initially linked with Leicester Medical School, Warwick Medical School experienced rapid growth and, in 2007, was granted independent degree-awarding status by the Privy Council on the recommendation of the General Medical Council of the United Kingdom. It is the only graduate-entry medical school in the UK. The school is organized into three institutes: the Institute of Clinical Education (ICE), which oversees undergraduate and postgraduate teaching; the Health Sciences Research Institute (HSRI); and the Clinical Sciences Research Institute (CSRI). The Institute of Clinical Education (ICE) Warwick Medical School offers a four-year Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (MB ChB) program, specifically designed for graduates in biological, natural, or physical sciences. Applicants must hold a strong academic degree (upper second class or above) or its equivalent. The program emphasizes early patient interaction and the development of clinical and communication skills from the outset. The MB ChB curriculum is divided into two phases. Phase I spans 18 months and focuses on academic learning through lectures and small group sessions led by clinicians or academic staff. Phase II is primarily clinical, consisting of 11 eight-week clinical blocks and an eight-week elective attachment. Clinical placements are conducted at three main hospitals: University Hospital Coventry and Warwickshire (UHCW), Warwick Hospital, and George Eliot Hospital. Additional placements occur in primary and community care settings, including general practices, outreach projects, and mental health services. Admissions to the MB ChB program begin with an application through UCAS, followed by the UK Clinical Aptitude Test. Selected applicants are invited to a selection center for interviews and team-based and written exercises. Final selection is based on performance at the selection center. In 2005, 900 applications were received, 300 candidates were interviewed, and 164 places were offered. Continuing Professional Development (CPD) Warwick Medical School has over 2,000 postgraduate students enrolled in CPD courses. These include Postgraduate Awards, Certificates, Diplomas, Master's Degrees, short courses, and non-accredited programs. Subject areas include child health, chronic disease management, dentistry, diabetes, public health, and occupational health. The school also offers a postgraduate program in Medical Education, equipping healthcare professionals with pedagogic skills for teaching and training in clinical environments. Research Degrees The school provides opportunities for research degrees, including a three-year full-time or five-year part-time PhD, a two-year full-time or three-year part-time MPhil, and an MSc by Research (one year full-time or two years part-time). Additionally, an MD (Doctor of Medicine) program is available, lasting two years full-time or three years part-time. Each student is supported by a supervisory team of at least two members, who meet regularly to ensure adequate guidance and monitoring. The school collaborates with various university departments, allowing students to benefit from interdisciplinary expertise. The Health Sciences Research Institute (HSRI) The HSRI focuses on community-oriented academic research and collaborates with several NHS trusts. It serves as the coordinating center for the Warwick and West Midlands Primary Care Research Network. Research areas include epidemiology, clinical trials, biostatistics, health economics, modeling, social sciences, and psychology. Key research themes include public mental health, emergency care and rehabilitation, cancer, and primary care. Emerging areas of focus include healthcare systems improvement. Warwick Clinical Trials Unit Established in 2005 within the HSRI, the Warwick Clinical Trials Unit specializes in designing and conducting clinical trials, particularly for complex health conditions and interventions. Its work encompasses musculoskeletal conditions, cancer, clinical trials methodology, and systematic reviews. The unit has grown significantly since its inception, and a new Clinical Trials Building is planned for the Gibbet Hill campus, supported by a £1 million grant from the Wolfson Foundation. The Clinical Sciences Research Institute (CSRI) The CSRI, located in a modern facility at University Hospital Coventry and Warwickshire, opened in 2005. It specializes in translational medicine, epidemiology, and clinical effectiveness. The institute houses 36 senior research academics and state-of-the-art equipment for molecular, cellular, proteomic, transcriptomic, and functional studies. Research themes align with the strategic priorities of University Hospital Coventry and Warwickshire, focusing on metabolic health (including obesity and diabetes), cardiovascular medicine, epidemiology, and reproductive health. History Warwick Medical School was initially established as a joint venture with the University of Leicester, forming the Leicester-Warwick Medical School. Professor Ian Lauder was appointed Dean of the joint school, and the first students arrived in September 2000. The school operated from temporary headquarters until the Medical Teaching Centre was completed in August 2001 and formally opened in 2002. In 2003, Professor Yvonne Carter became Vice-Dean and later Dean of Warwick Medical School. The first cohort of MB ChB students graduated in 2004, the same year the refurbished Medical School Building at Gibbet Hill was inaugurated. The Clinical Sciences Research Institute opened in 2005, followed by the Biomedical Learning Grid in 2006, equipped with advanced IT and traditional learning resources. In 2007, Warwick Medical School was granted independent degree-awarding status following an assessment by the General Medical Council. The first graduates to receive University of Warwick medical degrees completed their studies in the summer of 2007. Student-Led Projects In 2005, students initiated a project called Medics Without a Paddle to create an e-book containing free revision notes for Phase II clinical attachments. The material is entirely student-produced, with oversight by two student editors. This initiative fosters collaboration among students to share knowledge and experiences. The medical student community is supported by the University of Warwick MedSoc, which organizes social events, sports activities, and an annual Revue that humorously critiques the Medical School and the NHS. Phase I Assessments (2007) In 2007, one-third of the 185 students who took the Phase I end-of-year exam failed. After a retake, 35 students were unable to continue the course, with nine ultimately having their studies terminated. The high failure rate prompted an internal investigation by Warwick University. External examiners deemed the assessment fair and exemplary, but the school could not identify a specific reason for the increased failure rate. A Significant Event Review was conducted, and its findings were shared with students in May 2007. The school has since implemented recommendations from the review to improve the curriculum and assessment processes.
